newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine army chief to make key visit to Britain.
newsitem.headline: Argentine army chief to make key visit to Britain.

text.p: Argentina's army chief was set to become the highest-ranking officer since the Falklands war to visit London next month in a trip Britain considers a big step to warming relations, officials said on Monday.
A British Embassy official in Buenos Aires said Gen. Martin Balza, a Falklands veteran, was invited by Gen. Charles Guthrie, Chief of Britain's General Staff, to visit in mid-November.

"It's very significant," the official told Reuters. "We've been working hard to improve relations. It is a step-by-step process to improve confidence and this is an important step indeed in that way."

Britain and Argentina went to war over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, for 10 weeks in 1982. About 1,000 troops, most of them Argentine, died when Britain sent a task force to repel Argentine troops trying to enforce a 160-year-old sovereignty claim.
The two countries have since restored diplomatic links and have agreed on oil exploration in the South Atlantic.

Balza will visit military bases and meet defence ministry officials during the four or five day trip. He will be received by the honour guard, an act of protocol usually reserved for a head of state, the embassy official said.
Other Argentine generals have visited Britain but Balza, who was a lieutenant colonel during the conflict, is the highest ranking officer to travel there since the war.

His visit has additional significance for Britain because he formally apologised for his force's human rights abuses during the "dirty war" against Argentine leftists under junta rule from 1976-1983. Human rights groups believe up to 30,000 people died under the military's campaign.
Balza was also the only top commander to survive a shake-up of Argentina's military high command ordered last week.

A senior Foreign Office official this month said Britain still wanted Argentine President Carlos Menem to visit London but the time was not yet right. Talks on fishing in the South Atlantic have made little progress and Argentina feels that moves by Falkland Islanders to secure more autonomy would weaken its sovereignty claim.
